Learn about the steps that lead to U.S. citizenship, including the naturalization test. What are the requirements for U.S. citizenship? To be eligible for U.S. citizenship, you must meet certain eligibility requirements. These include being: At least 18 years old when you apply Able to read, write, and speak basic English (depending on age) Of good moral character You must also be in one of these categories: Lawful permanent resident (Green Card holder) of five years Married to a U.S. citizen and lawful permanent resident for three years U.S. military service member (active duty or veteran) Child of a U.S. citizen How to apply for U.S. citizenship Follow the 10-step naturalization process from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). You will learn: If you are eligible for naturalization How to fill out Form N-400 to apply for naturalization What to do before taking the oath of citizenship How long does the naturalization process take? pages.text: Beetles steal the scent of ants to secretly live among them | National Geographic ANIMALS Beetles steal the scent of ants to secretly live among them The catch? Once they enter the any colony, the beetles can never leave. Sceptobius beetles are seen grooming an ant as part of their evolved symbiotic relationship. D. Miller, Parker Lab/Caltech By Jason Bittel Published February 5, 2026 Life may look like a paradise for beetles living in ant colonies. Plump, wriggling ant larvae and helpless eggs sit waiting to be devoured, while hundreds of thousands of ants stand at the ready to ward off predators and parasites. There’s just one catch for these beetles, revealed in a new study published in the journal Cell . If one leaves the ant colony, it’ll be dead in less than a day. From bacteria living inside insect guts to mycorrhizal fungi on plant roots, symbiotic organisms abound across the tree of life, says Joseph Parker , an evolutionary biologist at the California Institute of Technology and senior author of the study. All these symbiotes have something in common that can also be a liability—their evolutionary entwinement has progressed so far, they can no longer live without their hosts. Parker and his colleagues wanted to know why. They tackled this question by investigating the odd relationship between a rove beetle known as Sceptobius lativentris and its host, the velvety tree ant. pages.description: The origin story has two settings: In Colorado, a gang of riders had the tenacity to conquer a treacherous terrain, and in California, others had the technology to design the ideal ride
pages.text: Before Mountain Biking Became One of the Most Popular Recreational Sports, Adventurous Souls of the American West Had to Invent a Rugged Bike Skip to main content Breeze’s earlier conceptual drawing for the Breezer 1 prototype. In the 1960s and ’70s, a countercultural movement drew a new generation of pioneers to the West. Suddenly, ski bums, scofflaws, draft dodgers and hippie homesteaders were joining the miners and hardscrabble farmers of mountain towns like Crested Butte, Colorado. Looking for a way to navigate both the Pontiac-bedeviling potholes in town as well as the dirt roads leading into the mountains, a small crew of Crested Butte transplants began building handmade off-road-ready bikes. They used a hodgepodge of vintage parts, in particular from World War II-era Schwinn bicycles. The group called itself the Grubstake Gang (named after a favorite watering hole), and they rejoiced when their heavy cruisers, outfitted with fat tires, proved capable of handling the punishing unpaved roads into and out of town. In September 1976, 15 cyclists attempted a seemingly impossible feat: riding these “klunkers” over 12,700-foot Pearl Pass to Aspen. The next day, just two riders rolled into Aspen; the steep Colorado stones of the 38-mile road had destroyed all the other klunkers. Around the same time, a group of teenagers in California’s Marin County—they called themselves the Larkspur Canyon Gang —were tinkering and racing their own garage-built bikes down the steep roads of Mount Tamalpais , north of San Francisco. Even Arkansans have largely forgotten that this attractive spa town was America’s original Sin City, teeming with casinos and brothels, and frequented by big-name gangsters. The mobster Bugsy Siegel may have even used Hot Springs as an inspiration when he was developing the Las Vegas Strip. The leading authority on the town’s colorful, decadent, sinful history (it was known as “the loose buckle in the Bible Belt”) is a charismatic, white-haired, sharp-dressed man named Robert K. Raines. A former rock singer and computer salesman, he has written a book and made several short documentaries about vice and organized crime in Hot Springs. pages.text: Ben Franklin Wasn’t Serious When He Implied the Wild Turkey Would Be a ‘Respectable’ National Symbol … but He Wasn’t Wrong, Either Skip to main content The head of a male turkey is distinguished by the colorful dewlap and caruncles on its neck. Joanna Lentini The wild turkey is a noble beast: the muscular, bronze-sheened ancestor of the barnyard turkeys we eat today. While the two technically belong to the same species, the barnyard variety is relatively new on the scene. People began domesticating wild turkeys in what is now Mexico more than 2,000 years ago, selectively breeding them over generations to become fat and docile. Wild turkeys, meanwhile, have inhabited North America for a much longer time—hundreds of thousands of years. Hunters still eat them, of course, and appreciate the lean gaminess of the wild flesh. But for most of us, the bird is less about sustenance than about a glimpse of the true national temperament: resourceful and restless, by turns noble and idiotic—as liable to swagger into view as to bolt for the trees. This feathery American character has long invited comparison with another native bird. When the Continental Congress first chose the bald eagle for our fledgling nation’s heraldry, Benjamin Franklin wrote to his daughter in 1784 condemning it as “a bird of bad moral character,” given to stealing food from smaller birds rather than hunting for itself. pages.text: Ben White: Declan Rice defends Arsenal team-mate after boos at Wembley - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Declan Rice joined Ben White at Arsenal after signing from West Ham in 2023 Published 14 November 2026 Declan Rice has defended Arsenal team-mate Ben White after the defender was booed at Wembley during England's 2-1 win over Croatia on Thursday. White, who came on as a substitute in the Nations League fixture, left the Three Lions' camp at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar to return home for personal reasons. He then made himself unavailable for selection for the rest of Gareth Southgate's reign. White was also booed by some fans in March's 1-1 draw with Ukraine after returning to the squad under Thomas Tuchel. "The incident with Ben was over five years ago, I don't know why it is still a conversation to be honest," Rice told BBC Radio 5 Live. "Knowing Ben, knowing the character he is, he has totally moved on from all of that. "He always wears the shirt with pride and every time he puts on the shirt, he gives 100 percent. "It shows his character. It is not easy being booed coming on at Wembley, but to show his mental strength to play the game and to play well, like he did in the previous months, is a real testament to him." Rice also said that the players do not discuss the situation at all and that everybody has moved on, adding that White has "an exciting future ahead with this England squad". By Nina Strochlic Published April 23, 2020 • 2 min read This story appears in the May 2020 issue of National Geographic magazine. When Beverly Goodman was in elementary school, she gave a series of presentations on her favorite topic: disasters. She told her classmates about the eruption that buried Pompeii , the black plague , and famous shipwrecks like the Titanic and the Lusitania . Today, at 45, she’s a marine geoarchaeologist who excavates coastlines for clues to erosion, past tsunamis , and other disasters. “It’s funny now that I’m a disaster scientist, basically,” she says. “It all came together.” Human settlements have long been built around access to water. Goodman studies how coastal change affected our ancestors: Were people forced to leave? Did they find innovative ways to adapt to the changes? This knowledge, she says, can help us “prepare responsibly for what this landscape is going to look like in the future.” That was the case when Goodman and her team of scientists proved tsunamis had struck the coast of what is now Israel over the course of thousands of years. Costs are often lower, while luxury accommodation can be similarly priced to budget options in mainstream European ski resorts. pages.text: Beyond the film festival—why Sundance is the ski resort to visit this year | National Geographic TRAVEL Beyond the film festival—why Sundance is the ski resort to visit this year Sundance Resort, founded by actor Robert Redford, has long been famed for its eco-conscious ethos and artistic crowd. But as the mountain village enters a new chapter — with expanded ski terrain and its first-ever hotel — can it retain its hometown charm? American actor Robert Redford fell in love with Mount Timpanogos and the surrounding area while driving his motorbike through Utah's Wasatch Mountains in 1961. Sundance Mountain Resort By Katja Gaskell Published April 18, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). “We’ve been skiing here since we were little kids,” says my chairlift companion, Devon. “We love it here.” I’m sitting on the four-seater Red’s Lift in Sundance Mountain Resort next to local brothers, Devon and Clovel Anderson, travelling the 2,515 metres up to Bearclaw Summit station on the slopes of Sundance’s highest peak, Mount Timpanogos. Wearing matching woolly hats, goggles and walrus moustaches, the sixtysomething siblings are diehard Sundance fans. “It’s my therapy,” says Clovel. “Skiing here feels like freedom.” With empty slopes and serene views of the Heber and Utah Valleys, and the surrounding Wasatch mountains, it does feel a world away from some of the state’s mega-resorts.
